lines.why: Words only, against 001-pilot. Nothing aired is a greeting of this kind, and no aired line wishes anyone a happy anything. The subject has been used once: the aired monologue named two of the cluster's themed weeks for a joke about both falling on one day, and the weather board had a blank week in its outlook. Here the week is this window's, the line makes no joke about how long a week lasts or how many there are, and nothing points back, so the subject returns with a different use. It is also not the aired way of signing off in the community's idiom: that was an abbreviation the night had made a runner of, paid off in five steps; this is one toast with no plant behind it in the show's own history. For the ledger: record the form as well as the words. The cluster names a week most weeks, so 'Happy <name> week.' can be refilled every episode, and the second time it is a line that is said every week.

Words only; the owner has ruled that a goodnight at the close is frame, so the act is not judged. The aired episode had two spoken goodnights from the host, and neither is this one. The first was a stock line (the ledger lists it) whose whole content was its address, a word that paid off a real post held on a card; the second was the two-letter abbreviation with the cluster's name, the payoff of the night's runner, followed by a post going viral and a confirming chyron. This line has neither address, spells the words out in full, has no joke in it and none set up for it: nothing says a goodnight is rare, late or hard to say, nothing counts it, and no card or post follows. So the old runner is not woken and the stock line is not heard; a viewer would not recognise either in it. Two cautions that do not make it a repeat. (1) 'everybody' was the host's tag word on three buttons in the aired episode. Once, here, as an address, is not a return anyone will hear, but it is what makes this the genre's default goodnight and not this week's. (2) Three goodnights in two episodes now have the form 'good night' plus a word for the audience. The frame covers saying goodnight; it does not cover a form. These exact words are spent after this episode, and next time a new address alone would be the same line with a new noun. For the staging, which is not mine to judge here: keep the abbreviation off the screen and make no point of the goodnight having been said.

Words only. No aired line is this one or a variant a viewer would know. The nearest aired things are two stock lines, the host's throw promising a great show and telling the audience to stay, and his line that the show was almost over. Both are generic late-night formulae with nothing of the night in them; this line says what the segment is (a game), counts on the two games before it, and names the one thing left. It works for someone who saw nothing earlier and refers to no earlier episode. One note for the record: 'the song', with the definite article, tells the viewer the show has one. Said once it is a join. If 'before the song' came back in another episode it would be treating the song as a fixture, which the frame does not make it.

inside: 'Happy polyhedra week.' answers the coffee segment, the only other place the week is named aloud (a member's own 'polyhedron week comes in many forms', which spells it differently), so it lands as a callback in a different voice and not a repeat; 'Good night, everybody.' is the host's second sign-off of the episode, after the making-of's 'And that's the show.' at the midpoint, and its long applause would be the second in under two minutes while the chess segment still ends on the sting and long applause it carried when it was the close.
